answer_text:
Let the numbers in clockwise order be  
\[
a_0,a_1,\dots,a_{n-1},
\]
with indices taken modulo \(n\). The condition is
\[
a_i=a_{i-1}a_{i+1}\qquad (i=0,1,\dots,n-1).
\]

### 1. No number can be \(0\)

Suppose \(a_k=0\). Then
\[
0=a_{k-1}a_{k+1},
\]
so at least one neighbor of \(a_k\) is also \(0\). Thus there are two adjacent zeros.

If \(a_j=a_{j+1}=0\), then
\[
a_{j+2}=a_{j+1}a_{j+3}=0.
\]
Iterating around the circle gives all numbers equal to \(0\), which is impossible because the \(n\) numbers must be distinct. Hence all \(a_i\neq 0\).

### 2. The sequence has period \(6\)

Since all terms are nonzero, we can rewrite the condition as
\[
a_{i+1}=\frac{a_i}{a_{i-1}}.
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{i+2}&=\frac{a_{i+1}}{a_i}
      =\frac{a_i/a_{i-1}}{a_i}
      =\frac1{a_{i-1}},\\[2mm]
a_{i+3}&=\frac{a_{i+2}}{a_{i+1}}
      =\frac{1/a_{i-1}}{a_i/a_{i-1}}
      =\frac1{a_i},\\[2mm]
a_{i+4}&=\frac{a_{i+3}}{a_{i+2}}
      =\frac{1/a_i}{1/a_{i-1}}
      =\frac{a_{i-1}}{a_i},\\[2mm]
a_{i+5}&=\frac{a_{i+4}}{a_{i+3}}
      =\frac{a_{i-1}/a_i}{1/a_i}
      =a_{i-1},\\[2mm]
a_{i+6}&=\frac{a_{i+5}}{a_{i+4}}
      =\frac{a_{i-1}}{a_{i-1}/a_i}
      =a_i.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
a_{i+6}=a_i
\]
for all \(i\).

### 3. The length \(n\) must divide \(6\)

The sequence is periodic with period \(n\) because it is arranged on a circle, and it is also periodic with period \(6\). Therefore it is periodic with period
\[
\gcd(n,6).
\]

If \(\gcd(n,6)<n\), then two entries of the circle would be equal, contradicting distinctness. Hence
\[
\gcd(n,6)=n,
\]
so \(n\mid 6\). Since \(n\ge 3\), the only possibilities are
\[
n=3 \quad\text{or}\quad n=6.
\]

### 4. Eliminate \(n=3\)

For \(n=3\), let the numbers be \(x,y,z\). Then
\[
x=yz,\qquad y=zx,\qquad z=xy.
\]
None can be \(0\). Multiplying the three equations gives
\[
xyz=(xyz)^2.
\]
Since \(xyz\neq 0\), we get \(xyz=1\). Then
\[
x=yz=\frac1x,
\]
so \(x^2=1\). Similarly \(y^2=z^2=1\). Thus each of \(x,y,z\) is either \(1\) or \(-1\), so they cannot be three distinct real numbers. Therefore \(n=3\) is impossible.

### 5. Show \(n=6\) is possible

Arrange the six distinct numbers
\[
2,\quad 3,\quad \frac32,\quad \frac12,\quad \frac13,\quad \frac23
\]
around the circle in that order. Check the neighbor products:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac23\cdot 3&=2,\\
2\cdot \frac32&=3,\\
3\cdot \frac12&=\frac32,\\
\frac32\cdot \frac13&=\frac12,\\
\frac12\cdot \frac23&=\frac13,\\
\frac13\cdot 2&=\frac23.
\end{aligned}
\]
Each number equals the product of its two immediate neighbors, and all six numbers are distinct.

Therefore the only possible value is

\[
\boxed{6}
\]
